questions.q: What is an adversarial example, precisely?
options: A malformed input that crashes the model's inference server
An input flagged by a web application firewall before it ever reaches the model
An input deliberately perturbed by a small, often human-imperceptible amount so the model misclassifies it
Any input the model was never trained on, regardless of how it looks
questions.explain: An adversarial example is well-formed and passes normal validation; the 'attack' is a property of the model's decision boundary, not a malformed or out-of-distribution input.

questions.q: What did the panda/gibbon result from Goodfellow, Shlens, and Szegedy (2014) actually demonstrate?
options: A classifier that correctly labeled a panda image mislabeled it as a gibbon after an imperceptible pixel-level perturbation was added
A classifier was retrained on gibbon images until it forgot what a panda looked like
A spam filter was evaded using a homoglyph character-substitution attack
A malware classifier was evaded by padding a binary file with junk bytes
questions.explain: The classic demonstration added a visually imperceptible perturbation to a correctly classified panda photo, flipping the model's high-confidence prediction to 'gibbon' with no change a human would notice.

questions.q: How does the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) actually construct a perturbation?
options: It randomly shuffles input values until the classifier's confidence drops below a threshold
It retrains the target model from scratch on adversarially labeled data
It queries the model thousands of times to brute-force a misclassification without any gradient information
It computes the gradient of the model's loss with respect to the input and nudges each input dimension slightly in the direction that increases loss
questions.explain: FGSM is a white-box, gradient-based attack: it uses the sign of the loss gradient with respect to the input to decide which direction to perturb each dimension.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a perturbation budget (epsilon), measured under a norm like L∞ or L2?
options: To guarantee the perturbed input will fool every other model trained on a similar task
To cap how large a perturbation is allowed to be, so the comparison between 'an adversarial example' and 'just a different input' stays honest
To encrypt the perturbation so it cannot be detected by a human reviewer
To set the learning rate used during the target model's original training run
questions.explain: The budget bounds perturbation size under a chosen norm. Without that bound, a large enough change stops being an imperceptible adversarial example and becomes simply a different, visibly different input.

questions.q: What does 'transferability' mean in adversarial ML research, and why does it matter to a defender?
options: An adversarial example crafted against one model often fools a different model trained on a similar task, even without access to that second model's internals
A model's clean accuracy improves automatically once adversarial examples are added to its training data
An adversarial example can only ever fool the exact model instance it was generated against
A black-box attacker must obtain the target model's full source code before an attack can succeed
questions.explain: Transferability means attacks developed against a surrogate model frequently work against the real target too, which is why keeping a model's internals secret is not, by itself, a reliable defense.
